blocks.text: We know that both heat and work correspond to transfer of energy by some means. The idea was first applied to the steam engine where it was natural to transfer heat in and get work out. Consequently, it made a sense to define both heat in and work out as positive quantities. Hence, work done by the system on its environment is considered positive while work done on the system by the environment is taken as negative. If an amount of heat Q enters the system, it could manifest itself as either an increase in internal energy or as a resulting quantity of work performed by the system on the surrounding or both.

We can express the work in terms of directly measurable variables. Consider the gas enclosed in the cylinder with a moveable, frictionless piston of cross-sectional area A (Fig.6.4-a). In equilibrium, the system occupies volume V, and exerts a pressure P on the walls of the cylinder and its piston. The force F exerted by the gas on the piston is PA.

blocks.alt: (a) A cylinder holding gas of pressure P and volume V, closed by a piston of area A; a downward force F acts on the piston rod. (b) The same cylinder standing on a hot plate: the piston has risen through delta y, shown between two dashed lines, and the gas now has volume V + delta V.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.4: A gas is sealed in a cylinder by a weightless, frictionless piston. The constant downward applied force F equals PA, and when the piston is displaced, downward work is done on the gas (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.4).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed caption says downward work is done on the gas, but panel (b) shows the gas expanding and pushing the piston up, so there the gas does work on the piston.

blocks.text: Knowing the details of the change in internal energy and the mechanical work done, we are in a position to describe the general principles which deal with heat energy and its transformation into mechanical energy. These principles are known as laws of thermodynamics.
